records.p: This reddish-brown snake has a pointed snout, rounded prominent eyes and fifteen dorsal scale rows at midbody (Sanguila et al., 2026). A reddish body, pointed snout and fifteen midbody dorsal scale rows were reported (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Philippine Shrub Snake has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026). The Philippine Shrub Snake was recorded in ground-level habitats in the Taguibo Watershed of Mindanao (Sanguila et al., 2021). The northeastern Leyte team observed nighttime activity: snakes were on the ground or coiled on leaves and shrubs, with juveniles among the individuals using elevated foliage (Decena et al., 2023). Northeastern Leyte researchers recorded three individuals in forest and agricultural settings, with night encounters involving juveniles coiled on leaves and other snakes moving through shrubs or across the ground. These observations demonstrate both arboreal and ground-level activity but not their relative frequencies across the species’ range (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The diagnosis notes a single scale behind the eye, incomplete snout-scale sutures and 20–23 scales around midbody; the species has the elongate, externally limbless form of a blind skink (Uetz et al., 2026). The White Blind Legless Lizard is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Lumot and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The White Blind Legless Lizard is broadly associated with forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The type series and subsequent accounts have used several older combinations for this limb-reduced lizard, including Dibamus argenteus as a historical name associated with material from the Butuan region. These names need comparison with the original diagnoses before merging occurrence records (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Philippine snake key uses the spelling Calliophis philippina for this form. It describes pale lengthwise stripes along the back and black ventral bands that meet the black lateral surface. Cream-colored bands on the underside extend up the body sides, often as far as the fourth dorsal scale row, unlike the lower, shorter side bars of C. suluensis (Weinell et al., 2019). The Philippine Coral Snake has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Lumot, Mount Bato, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Coral Snake was recorded in ground-level habitats in the Taguibo Watershed of Mindanao (Sanguila et al., 2021). Egg laying is reported for this coral snake (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A large coral snake with a black head, alternating broad dark and off-white body bands, and an unbanded orange tail. The original Dinagat specimen was 997 mm in total length (Brown et al., 2018). The Dinagat Coral Snake is recorded on Dinagat (GBIF.org, 2026). The type specimen was collected at night beside a forested stream on Mount Cambinlia, Dinagat Island (Brown et al., 2018). The type specimen was encountered at night, during approximately 19:00–22:00 field searches, near a forest stream at Mt. Cambinlia, Dinagat Island (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Turtle-headed Seasnake has an unusual enlarged, tooth-like scale on each side of the upper lip, associated with scraping fish eggs from reef surfaces. This feature is documented in the Smithsonian’s species account and can help recognize the specialized head profile. Colour patterns and reliable separation from other marine snakes require an illustrated key and specialist examination (Smithsonian Ocean, 2015). The Turtle-headed Seasnake is recorded on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Turtle-headed Seasnake is associated with coastal and intertidal habitats as well as marine waters. This sea snake is specialized for feeding on fish eggs and is live-bearing (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

r.full: Smithsonian Ocean. (2015). A turtle or a sea snake? https://ocean.si.edu/ocean-life/reptiles/turtle-or-sea-snake

records.p: The published diagnosis gives 25–30 scale rows around the neck, 39–49 at midbody, and usually a dark olive to black head and forebody with pale, oval, yellowish lateral spots; complete annuli may occur in juveniles. No single color character is sufficient for identification (Uetz et al., 2026). The Black-headed Sea Snake has historical reports from marine waters around Mindanao and Samar. Those records have not all been confirmed under modern species identifications (Leviton et al., 2018; Sanguila et al., 2016). The Black-headed Sea Snake is associated with marine waters. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Scale counts in the compiled diagnosis are 23–35 around the neck and 25–43 around the body. The lowermost three or four lateral scale rows are larger than adjacent rows, and dark dorsal crossbands may meet beneath the body (Uetz et al., 2026). The Short Sea Snake is recorded from coastal waters off the Zamboanga Peninsula in western Mindanao (Leviton et al., 2018). The Short Sea Snake is broadly associated with marine waters. The species is live-bearing, rather than laying eggs on land (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The diagnostic compilation gives 27–35 neck-scale rows and 37–47 body-scale rows. The dark bluish or black bands vary in breadth and can encircle the body; band definition may fade with age, making coloration alone unreliable (Uetz et al., 2026). Live-bearing reproduction is reported for this marine sea snake (Uetz et al., 2026). The Annulated Sea Snake has records from Basilan (GBIF.org, 2026). The Annulated Sea Snake is broadly associated with marine waters. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A contrasting dark upper body and yellow ventral region are characteristic of this pelagic sea snake (Uetz et al., 2026). The Yellow-bellied Sea Snake has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Yellow-bellied Sea Snake lives mainly in open ocean waters, often associated with surface slicks. It is fully marine and gives birth to live young at sea (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Yellow-lipped Sea Krait has a yellow upper lip, alternating dark and pale body bands, laterally placed nostrils and a laterally compressed tail. The diagnosis summarized by The Reptile Database describes 21–25 rows of body scales at midbody and broad ventral scales occupying a substantial part of the underside (The Reptile Database, 2026). The Yellow-lipped Sea Krait has been documented on Leyte, including Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013). The Yellow-lipped Sea Krait is associated with coastal and intertidal habitats. The category does not distinguish time spent at sea from access to coastal terrestrial resting or egg-laying sites. This amphibious sea krait returns to land to lay eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Blue-lipped sea kraits have a banded body and relatively narrow, paddle-shaped tail but must be distinguished from other Laticauda by head coloration and scale characters. In contrast to fully pelagic sea snakes, they possess enlarged ventral scales that permit crawling ashore (Uetz et al., 2026). The Blue-lipped Sea Krait is documented along the coastal reefs of Zamboanga del Norte, western Mindanao (Bucol et al., 2026). The Blue-lipped Sea Krait is associated with coastal and intertidal habitats. The category does not distinguish time spent at sea from access to coastal terrestrial resting or egg-laying sites. This sea krait lays eggs on land rather than bearing its young in seawater (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Published characters include 195–205 ventral scales, 21–23 scale rows around the neck and body, and 38–43 paired subcaudals in males compared with 32–36 in females. These are comparative characters, not a complete diagnostic key (Uetz et al., 2026). The Half-banded Sea Krait has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga Peninsula (GBIF.org, 2026). The Half-banded Sea Krait is broadly associated with coastal and intertidal habitats. Females lay eggs on land (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The published key notes yellow anterior ventrals followed by a dark band and 162–178 ventral scales (Weinell et al., 2019). The 2019 Philippine snake key gives 17–19 midbody scale rows and a dark brown or black dorsal surface (Weinell et al., 2019). A dark cobra with pale throat scales and a broad dark band across the anterior underside (Plaza et al., 2025). Some individuals exhibit a faint pale line along the anterior outermost dorsal scale rows. The Tinuy-an Falls identification gives 21–23 rows around the neck, narrowing to 19 rows at midbody (Plaza et al., 2025). The Hijo Forest account notes the defensive hood and predominantly yellowish to dark body color as field-visible characters; reliable identification requires more than hood shape alone (Gamalo et al., 2023). The Southern Philippine Cobra is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Leyte, including Mount Agad-Agad on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; GIZ, 2013; The Reptile Database, n.d.; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Southern Philippine Cobra has been observed on open ground beside streams in eastern Mindanao (Plaza et al., 2025). A Samar Cobra attempting to take a Banded Bullfrog (Kaloula pulchra) was documented on Mindanao (Caasi, 2024). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). In Hijo Forest, observers documented this cobra opportunistically during daytime field visits (Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: A 2016 review describes the eastern Mindanao distribution established in the 2010 revision. Specimens were found among stream-bank boulders, stream vegetation, and in one cave (Brown et al., 2016). The reptile account cites Mindanao, Leyte, and Dinagat, with older Gymnodactylus combinations (The Reptile Database, n.d.). The 2010 revision distinguishes C. agusanensis from C. gubaot by sampled midbody dorsal scales (111–124 versus 92–105), paravertebral scales (184–196 versus 150–162), and postcloacal lateral tubercles (8–11 versus 4–6) (Welton et al., 2010). The original diagnosis describes strongly pointed enlarged dorsal tubercles arranged in irregular longitudinal rows and tuberculate rings on the tail (Uetz et al., 2026). The Agusan Bent-toed Gecko is documented on eastern Mindanao. Older reports from Leyte and Dinagat were made under a wider Cyrtodactylus agusanensis species-complex concept, and their assignment differs among later sources (Sanguila et al., 2016; Uetz et al., 2026). The 2016 northeast Mindanao herpetofauna survey collected Cyrtodactylus agusanensis among boulders along stream banks at surveyed eastern Mindanao sites (Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in ground-level habitats (Sanguila et al., 2021). The northeast Mindanao survey reports Cyrtodactylus agusanensis from eastern Mindanao under the taxonomic treatment revised in 2010, not from the entire older Mindanao–Leyte–Dinagat species complex (Sanguila et al., 2016). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: Three dark transverse body bands have a narrow barbell-like shape, in contrast to the four or five bow-tie-like bands of the Palawan C. tautbatorum (Uetz et al., 2026). The Annulated Bent-toed Gecko is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023; Tirona et al., 2026). Specimens occupied tree trunks in peat and freshwater swamp forest at Agusan Marsh (Sanguila et al., 2026). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in vegetation and trees (Sanguila et al., 2021). During the northeastern Leyte study, geckos were active at night on tree trunks or branches and along stream boulders; daytime sheltering was reported in rock fissures and log piles (Decena et al., 2023). Northeastern Leyte individuals were encountered at night on tree trunks and branches up to about 2.5 m above ground and on streamside logs and boulders; by day they were noted hiding in rock crevices or piles of logs. These are documented microhabitats and activity observations, not detection-corrected habitat selection (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Adults reported from the type series measure 85.6–100.1 mm snout–vent length; a dark-gray belly with pale flecks and conspicuous dark canthal stripe distinguish it from the smaller Samar C. sumuroi (Uetz et al., 2026). The Leyte Bent-toed Gecko is recorded on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in vegetation and trees (Decena et al., 2023). One individual was found between rocks beside a stream in relatively undisturbed dipterocarp forest on Leyte (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The original description includes lavender-brown dorsal marbling, pale yellow spotting on tubercles and near the eyes, and the absence of enlarged femoral pore-bearing scales (Uetz et al., 2026). Additional characters from the formal diagnosis include pale yellow supraciliary markings, a canthal stripe and a male inverted V-shaped arrangement of precloacal pores. These need to be considered jointly with dorsal markings and scalation to distinguish similar bent-toed geckos (Uetz et al., 2026). The Zamboanga Bent-toed Gecko has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area (GBIF.org, 2026). The type specimen was encountered at night on a sapling trunk in Pasonanca Natural Park, Zamboanga City (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Dinagat species has a pale belly, relatively small head tubercles, no dark canthal stripe and dark dorsal bands surrounding paler bands (Uetz et al., 2026). The Unib Island study illustrates a specimen with an unusually trifurcated regenerated tail, reported as an individual developmental abnormality. Tail trifurcation is not a normal diagnostic feature of the species (Maglangit et al., 2021). The Mamanwa Bent-toed Gecko is documented on Dinagat and neighboring Unib Island. The 2026 national reptile checklist also lists Siargao, but the previously stated mainland Mindanao occurrence is not supported by the specialist records reviewed (Maglangit et al., 2021; Uetz et al., 2026). On Unib Island in the Dinagat group, investigators observed nocturnal foraging on cockroaches, termites and other small arthropods in karst habitats. They recorded lizards on rock faces, crevices and trunks by night and under logs, among branches and on cave walls by day (Maglangit et al., 2021). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The diagnosis records 87–98 dorsal scale rows and a canthal stripe; the comparable C. agusanensis has 111–124 dorsal scale rows in the cited comparison (Uetz et al., 2026). The Samar species has a pale cream belly and a relatively short reported snout–vent length of 73.9–84.9 mm; dark dorsal bands enclose lighter areas (Uetz et al., 2026). The Sumuroy's Bent-toed Gecko has been documented on Samar, including Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). During the type-series collections in Taft Forest, Eastern Samar, individuals were observed between 18:00 and 22:00 on shrubs or young saplings approximately 1–2 m above ground in secondary-growth forest. This is localized nocturnal perch evidence, not a measured preferred perch height across the range (Welton et al., 2010). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The rounded adhesive toe pads and thick, flattened-underneath tail distinguish this house gecko (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Tender-skinned Gecko; Common Four-toed Gecko has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Lumot, Misamis Oriental, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Tender-skinned Gecko was recorded in vegetation and trees in the Taguibo Watershed of Mindanao (Sanguila et al., 2021). It frequents darker tree surfaces and structures rather than gathering around artificial lights (Sanguila et al., 2026). In Agusan Marsh, individuals occupied sheltered trees and buildings away from bright lights (Sanguila et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Tokay Gecko is a robust, large-headed gecko with conspicuous rounded orange to reddish spots on a bluish-grey or grey body. Its prominent eyes have vertical pupils, and the expanded toe pads bear adhesive lamellae. The intensity of the background colour varies, so the body pattern should be considered together with size and structure (Smithsonian National Zoo, n.d.). The Tokay Gecko is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Malindang Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Gamalo et al., 2023). In the Leyte Cordillera and Babatngon ranges, the species was encountered in vegetation and trees (Decena et al., 2023). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The tokay gecko was detected acoustically in Hijo Forest: calls were heard but no individual was visually observed during the study’s fieldwork (Gamalo et al., 2023). In the northeastern Leyte herpetofaunal survey, a single animal was observed on a tree trunk approximately 5 m above ground in an isolated residential area. This records an observed perch and the survey’s limited coverage of settlements, rather than an estimate of urban abundance (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

r.full: Smithsonian National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute. (n.d.). Tokay gecko (Gekko gecko): physical description. https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/tokay-gecko

records.p: Descriptions mention 10–12 irregular longitudinal rows of flattened dorsal tubercles, with flaps of skin along the tail (Uetz et al., 2026). The Philippine Parachute Gecko is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range and Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). One intermediate flying gecko was observed in a firing-range shed within the Hijo forest, indicating use of that constructed shelter at this locality (Gamalo et al., 2023). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

A relatively small Gekko (reported snout–vent length up to about 86 mm in the 2006 comparison), generally brown to olive-brown with darker paired markings along the back and scattered enlarged dorsal tubercles. Adult males have an extended series of preanofemoral pores, and scale counts and arrangement of caudal tubercles help distinguish it from the similar G. ernstkelleri of Panay. Characters were evaluated in preserved specimens outside the disputed eastern Mindanao records; Greater Mindanao identifications labelled G. cf. mindorensis should remain provisional until specimen-level comparison (Rösler et al., 2006). The Mindoro Narrow-disked Gecko is listed from Mindanao in specialist range summaries. Reports from the Mount Hamiguitan area and Dinagat remain uncertain under the current species concept, while a provisional Camiguin identification lies outside this volume’s PAIC (Sanguila et al., 2016; Uetz et al., 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The regional checklist lists forest for the Mindoro Narrow-disked Gecko, but its reported Greater Mindanao identifications remain disputed. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Gekko mindorensis is the type species of the subgenus Archipelagekko. Older Mindanao material includes specimens reported as Gekko cf. mindorensis (Wood et al., 2019, 2020; Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: This gecko has broad adhesive pads beneath the digits, enlarged flattened tubercles on the back, and a cylindrical tail bearing raised dorsal tubercles (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Common House Gecko has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Surigao del Norte, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023; Tirona et al., 2026). The Common House Gecko frequently occurs around homes and other disturbed habitats. It has also been recorded on vines and branches above swamp water in Agusan Marsh (Sanguila et al., 2016; Sanguila et al., 2021; Sanguila et al., 2026). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The body has thin lateral skin flanges and a conspicuously flattened, expanded tail. These features distinguish it from the Common House Gecko, H. frenatus, which has a rounded tail and lacks the expanded flank folds (Brown et al., 2013). The Flat-tailed House Gecko has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Agad-Agad, Misamis Occidental, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Beukema, 2011). The Flat-tailed House Gecko is associated with settlements and disturbed areas. Egg laying is recorded for the Flat-tailed House Gecko (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: In a morphological comparison that included five Philippine females, Hemidactylus stejnegeri had a strongly depressed head and body, an elongated snout and no enlarged dorsal tubercles. The paired anterior postmental scales are larger and contact one another and the adjacent lower-lip scales; the posterior pair is separated by small scales. Adhesive scansors extend along the undersides of the digits, with several subterminal scansors divided or deeply notched. The original tail has serrated lateral edges but lacks broad skin flanges. The five Philippine females measured 54.5–60.2 mm snout–vent length; this is a small sample, not a species-wide limit (Ota et al., 1993). Stejneger’s Leaf-toed Gecko has been documented from Mindanao, including museum specimens examined in a comparative study of Philippine populations (Ota et al., 1993). The Stejneger's House Gecko is associated with forests, settlements, and other disturbed areas. This gecko has documented triploid parthenogenetic populations, allowing egg production without fertilization (Uetz et al., 2026). Hemidactylus stejnegeri was described by Ota and Hikida in 1989 and had previously been treated within the H. garnotii–vietnamensis complex (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A very small slender gecko with mostly granular body scales, expanded adhesive toe pads and a conspicuous dark, approximately pentagonal marking immediately behind the hips. In the Philippine voucher series examined by Zug (2010), this postsacral marking was edged by paler areas, and living individuals had reddish dorsolateral spots. Adult males had separate series of precloacal and femoral pores, whereas adult females lacked them. Observed snout–vent lengths were 28.8–34.4 mm for 19 males and 29.6–37.3 mm for 15 females; these are sample ranges, not absolute limits. Scale and pore characters are needed to distinguish similar slender geckos (Zug, 2010). The Philippine Slender Gecko has been reported from Mindanao. Some Mindanao identifications remain subject to taxonomic reassessment. Reports from the Sulu Archipelago lie outside the Greater Mindanao PAIC (Zug, 2010; Sanguila et al., 2016; Uetz et al., 2026). The Philippine Slender Gecko is broadly associated with forests, rivers, streams, caves and karst areas. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Hemiphyllodactylus insularis was formerly included in the broader H. typus complex before being recognized as a separate species (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The body is very slender, with a dark stripe extending from the eye toward the trunk, a pale band near the base of the tail, and divided adhesive scales near the digit tips (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Indo-Pacific Slender Gecko has records from Mindanao, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Sinaka and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Indo-Pacific Slender Gecko is listed from forest and freshwater-wetland settings in the regional checklist. The species includes parthenogenetic lineages. Parthenogenetic reproduction is documented; females can reproduce without mating (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A golden stripe extends from the snout past the eye toward the back of the head, and the underside of the tail is flattened (Uetz et al., 2026). Taylor’s original type diagnosis reports a continuous, angular row of preanal and femoral pores, numbering 19 on each side, together with a laterally edged tail. Pore configuration adds an anatomical check beyond the already-described golden lateral stripe (Uetz et al., 2026). The Mindanao Yellow Smooth-scaled Gecko is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Yellow Smooth-scaled Gecko is listed from freshwater wetland environments in the regional checklist. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This scaly-toed gecko has a rostral scale contacting the nostril and relatively few dorsal scales across the midbody. In the comparative series examined by Eliades et al. (2021), the two named forms, L. herrei herrei and L. herrei medianus, had 9–11 and 11–14 midbody dorsal scales, respectively. Adult males had 31–37 and 33–39 precloacofemoral pores, respectively. The recorded adult snout–vent lengths were 41.6–50.8 mm and 38.1–44.7 mm. These are measurements from the reviewed Negros and Cebu specimen series, not measurements newly verified for Mindanao records. Species-level recognition requires multiple scale characters (Eliades et al., 2021). The Negros Scaly-toed Gecko has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Agad-Agad and Lanao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; GIZ, 2013). The Negros Scaly-toed Gecko is associated with forests and freshwater wetlands. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026).

The comparative Philippine series of Lepidodactylus labialis examined by Eliades et al. (2021) had adult snout–vent lengths of 42.5–52.8 mm and 18–24 dorsal scales across the midbody. In the males examined, 11–13 precloacofemoral pores form a V-shaped series. Its rostral scale contacts the nostril and is cleft; cloacal spurs were absent in the comparisons, and there was no webbing between Toes II and III. The combination of rostral structure, pore arrangement and toe characters is more useful than general body colour alone (Eliades et al., 2021). The Mindanao Smooth-scaled Gecko is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hilong-Hilong and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Smooth-scaled Gecko is broadly associated with forests, cultivated land, and settlements and disturbed habitats. The species is an egg-laying gecko (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A small, smooth-scaled gecko with a greyish-tan to brown upper surface, often showing dark spots or irregular chevrons between the forelimbs and hindlimbs. A dark stripe may extend from the snout through the eye toward the shoulder. The toes have moderately expanded pads with divided terminal scansors, and the markings vary among parthenogenetic lineages (Siler, n.d., citing Brown and Alcala, 1978). The Mangrove Smooth-scaled Gecko has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mangrove Smooth-scaled Gecko is associated with forest, cultivated land and settlements and includes parthenogenetic lineages (Uetz et al., 2026). The Mourning Gecko reproduces mainly through parthenogenesis. Both diploid and triploid lineages have been described (Uetz et al., 2026). Published reproductive studies describe females producing offspring without fertilization, the parthenogenetic breeding mode characteristic of this gecko (Uetz et al., 2026). Published reproductive accounts distinguish all-female parthenogenetic lineages from rarer sexual or mixed populations of the mourning gecko. Therefore, the occurrence of eggs or several females in one shelter does not by itself establish a species-wide reproductive mode or a local breeding population (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A small gecko with an unusually broad, strongly flattened tail bordered by a free, flap-like lateral margin. Its digits are relatively broad. The original description compares these characters with the narrower, more gradually tapering tail and slimmer digits of L. lugubris (Stejneger, 1905). The species was originally described from a Mount Apo specimen on Mindanao. The working occurrence compilation also reports Samar and Bohol, but those records have not been reconciled against the original diagnosis (Stejneger, 1905; GBIF.org, 2026). The Flat-tailed Smooth-scaled Gecko is associated with montane environments. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: An exceptionally small forest gecko in the comparative Philippine Luperosaurus material, with a robust body, conspicuous conical or spine-like dorsal and dorsolateral tubercles, lateral tail tubercles, a narrow ear opening and substantial webbing between the fingers and toes. Brown, Diesmos and Duya (2007) report 27.5–32.4 mm snout–vent length from only two examined specimens, including a possibly immature paratype, and describe roughly one-half to two-thirds webbing between the middle digits. The combination of very small size, extensive webbing, enlarged tubercles and a narrow ear opening distinguishes the reviewed specimens from many congeners. Exact pore counts are excluded here because the paper’s prose and comparative table disagree slightly on their allocation to joloensis and palawanensis. The scant material limits confident extrapolation across age classes or unexamined populations. The Jolo Wolf Gecko has records from southwestern Mindanao and from Jolo in the Sulu Archipelago, outside the Greater Mindanao PAIC. Its generic classification has also varied among taxonomic treatments (Meneses & Brown, 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Jolo Wolf Gecko is associated with forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The original holotype from Jolo Island is reported as lost during World War II. This limits direct comparison with the historic type and increases the importance of examining original descriptive characters when evaluating new specimens (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A small Philippine false gecko with conspicuous pale spots along the back and sides and a contrasting band between the eyes. In the examined series, the limbs lack prominent spots and the tail lacks distinct bands. Separation from similar false geckos also depends on head and scale characters (Davis et al., 2015). The Short-footed False Gecko is recorded on Bohol and Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Brown et al., 2020). The Short-footed False Gecko is broadly associated with forests, rivers, streams, caves and karst areas. Egg-laying reproduction is recorded (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A small gecko (recorded snout–vent length 54.7–55.9 mm) with pale brown body, conspicuous neon-green head, back and limb spots, and a banded tail; the original diagnosis reports no body stripes (Uetz et al., 2026). The Zamboanga False Gecko is documented on the Zamboanga Peninsula of Mindanao. A previously listed Samar occurrence is not supported by the published specimen distribution or current specialist species summary (Uetz et al., 2026). This gecko has been recorded in secondary-growth forest near Zamboanga City (Uetz et al., 2026). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Small adult forest gecko reported at 49.4–52.6 mm snout–vent length, pale brown with no conspicuous head spotting or tail bands and 16–17 expanded scales under Toe IV (Uetz et al., 2026). The Leyte Diminutive False Gecko has been documented on Samar and Leyte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Brown et al., 2020). The described material includes specimens encountered at night in lowland secondary forest on Leyte (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Adult snout–vent length 66.6–76.8 mm; a striped gray-brown body, unspotted head and tail, and 17–21 expanded scales beneath Toe IV characterize the species (Uetz et al., 2026). The Southern Philippine False Gecko has been documented on Mindanao, Bohol, Dinagat, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Bega Watershed, Mount Lumot, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Uetz et al., 2026). Type-series individuals were found on a decaying stump and on the forest floor near bamboo in Bohol (Uetz et al., 2026). In the Leyte Cordillera and Babatngon ranges, the species was encountered in vegetation and trees (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This slender worm snake has a rounded snout, no subocular scales, nasal shields meeting behind the rostral (Uetz et al., 2026). A useful comparison with similar Philippine worm snakes is the approximately 18 longitudinal scale rows around midbody described in G. hedraeus, versus 20 reported for Ramphotyphlops olivaceus and 22 for R. suluensis in original comparative treatments. These are literature-reported differences that require correct species concept and intact specimens (Uetz et al., 2026). The Negros Island Worm Snake has been documented on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Negros Island Worm Snake is broadly associated with forests. This blind snake lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Southeast Asian Bockadam has a broad head with flattened scales on its crown and a mottled belly. The diagnosis transcribed by The Reptile Database gives 23, rarely 25, midbody scale rows, thin crown shields without keels in front of the jaw angle, and a horizontally divided last upper labial. These scalation characters provide more reliable comparisons than body colour alone (The Reptile Database, 2026). The Schneider's Dog-faced Water Snake has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Agad-Agad and Lanao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022). A coastal and estuarine snake associated with brackish water and mangrove habitats (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Crab-eating Water Snake has a short, smoothly rounded head that is not sharply differentiated from its stout cylindrical body, and a relatively short tail. Its upperbody is dark purplish brown, grading to pale or whitish below; the body scales are smooth. The head-neck shape and body proportions are useful external characters, but reliable distinction from other homalopsid watersnakes may require scale counts and careful head inspection (Singapore NParks, 2019). The Crab-eating Water Snake is recorded from Mindanao (Uetz et al., 2026). The crab-eating watersnake feeds heavily on crabs in coastal mangrove and mudflat habitats (Uetz et al., 2026). The name Fordonia leucobalia derives from the earlier combination Homalopsis leucobalia and is associated with several historic names, including Fordonia unicolor and Fordonia bicolor. This synonymy must be reconciled when compiling older specimen records (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This slender snake has a laterally compressed head with a blunt, nearly square snout and irregular brown, tan, and black markings. Its smooth dorsal scales form 13 rows at midbody (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Blunthead Slug Snake has records from Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Malindang Range, Cabadbaran–Santiago forest, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Magdiwata, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017). The Blunthead Slug Snake has been found in vegetation and trees within the protected landscape (Plaza et al., 2025). After rain, snakes hunted tree-dwelling slugs and snails near forest streams (Sanguila et al., 2016). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The original identification treatment describes a comparatively broad blunt snout, two preocular and two postocular scales, usually eight upper labials and smooth dorsal scales (Plaza et al., 2025). The Common Mock Viper is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Magdiwata, and Zamboanga del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026). Adults searched the ground while juveniles were found sleeping on saplings (Sanguila et al., 2016). The northeastern Leyte study observed individuals coiled on fern fronds during nocturnal searches in montane and lowland dipterocarp forest. The study reported sites between approximately 145 and 1,101 m elevation; these observations describe encounter habitats rather than an experimentally demonstrated habitat preference (Decena et al., 2023).

The lower lip bears heat-sensitive pits set within a longitudinal groove; the upper lip pits are less prominent, a diagnostic feature of Malayopython relative to Python (Uetz et al., 2026). The Reticulated Python has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Agad-Agad, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Supsup et al., 2017; Gamalo et al., 2023). The regional survey documented a nighttime record in a cultivated area (Sanguila et al., 2016). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The Hijo study records no visual encounter by the survey team, but describes multiple reports from forest guards and management, including a road incident involving a stray dog. These reports must not be represented as voucher-confirmed survey detections (Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The reported adult snout–vent length is 83.8–93.6 mm. Limbs retain five digits, and dark back stripes contrast with paler dorsolateral stripes (Uetz et al., 2026). The published diagnosis additionally describes 26–30 midbody scale rows (Uetz et al., 2026). The Bohol Slender Skink has been documented on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). This semifossorial skink has been recorded in leaf litter, loose soil and decaying wood on Bohol (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The reported snout–vent length spans 58.6–83.4 mm, with five digits on the limbs (Uetz et al., 2026). The species diagnosis gives 24–27 scales around midbody and a relatively long tail (Uetz et al., 2026). The Graceful Slender Skink is documented from Mindanao. Older occurrences attributed to this name elsewhere in Greater Mindanao need reassessment following revisions of the Brachymeles gracilis complex (Sanguila et al., 2016; Uetz et al., 2026). The Graceful Slender Skink is associated with forest, although earlier island reports may refer to other members of the species complex following taxonomic revision. Ovoviviparous reproduction is documented (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A short-limbed, slender skink with five digits on each hand and foot, visible ear openings, separate supranasal and prefrontal scales, and a small pineal eyespot. Scale counts and other characters are needed to distinguish it reliably from similar five-digited Brachymeles (Siler et al., 2012; Uetz et al., 2026). The Mindanao five-digited Slender Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Lumot, Surigao del Norte, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026). The species occurs in lowland secondary forest and disturbed habitats of northeastern Mindanao. It shelters among leaf litter, rotting logs, buttress roots, and decaying coconut piles. Taguibo Watershed records also document ground-level habitat use (Sanguila et al., 2016, 2021). The 2026 Samar checklist excludes historic Samar assignments and treats this species as restricted to Mindanao (Diesmos et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This small, slender skink measures 52.7–66.1 mm in snout–vent length in the cited description. It has an elongated body, reduced limbs bearing three digits each, and no externally visible ear opening (Uetz et al., 2026). The Lapinig Islands Slender Skink is documented from small offshore islands near Bohol, including the Lapinig group. These records do not establish its occurrence on Bohol’s main island (Siler et al., 2011; Uetz et al., 2026). The Lapinig Slender Skink shelters in forest-floor leaf litter and decomposing coconut husks in secondary-growth forest on Bohol (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This skink lacks dorsal stripes and retains a visible external ear opening (Plaza et al., 2025). The long-bodied, five-digit form is reported at 97.6–112.3 mm snout–vent length and lacks contrasting pale dorsolateral stripes (Uetz et al., 2026). The Southern Philippine Burrowing Skink is documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol and Dinagat. Reports from Camiguin concern an island outside the Greater Mindanao PAIC (Sanguila et al., 2016; Uetz et al., 2026). The Southern Philippine Burrowing Skink lives among soil, leaf litter and decaying vegetation, including stream margins and coconut plantations (Plaza et al., 2025; Sanguila et al., 2016). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The species is described with three-digit limbs and a snout–vent length of approximately 47.2–66.1 mm (Uetz et al., 2026). The original diagnosis also reports an externally concealed ear and largely uniform body coloration (Uetz et al., 2026). The PAEF Slender Skink has been documented on Leyte, including Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). This semifossorial skink is associated with decomposing logs and leaf litter (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Three examined adults measured 58–61 mm in snout–vent length. The species has reduced forelimbs with five vestigial digits, four hindlimb digits, a minute ear opening, 22–23 midbody scale rows and approximately six longitudinal rows of dark dorsal spots (Siler et al., 2011; Uetz et al., 2026). The Pathfinder Short-legged Skink has been documented from the Glan area of Sarangani in southern Mindanao, including historical collections under the former administrative designation of Cotabato (Taylor, 1925; Siler et al., 2011). The original collections document a semifossorial leaf-litter habitat (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The described individuals measure 64.2–76.9 mm snout–vent length and retain five digits on each limb (Uetz et al., 2026). The pale pineal eyespot and 25–26 rows of scales at midbody distinguish specimens in the original diagnosis (Uetz et al., 2026). The Eastern Visayas Slender Skink has records from Samar and Leyte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Eastern Visayas Slender Skink has been found beneath decomposing coconut husks in secondary forest on Samar (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A small slender skink, 57.9–66.1 mm snout–vent length, with two-toed reduced limbs (Uetz et al., 2026). In addition to two-digit limbs, this very small skink has no exposed ear opening and relatively uniform body coloration (Uetz et al., 2026). The Samar Slender Skink has been documented on Samar, including Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The species shelters beneath rotting logs and forest leaf litter (Uetz et al., 2026). The original Brachymeles samarensis series includes individuals located in rotten logs and leaf-litter shelters on Samar (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The relatively large reported body length is 93.1–115.8 mm snout–vent length, with five digits and no continuous bright dorsolateral stripes (Uetz et al., 2026). The Schadenberg's Slender Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Bato, and Zamboanga del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017). Field records place this relatively large semifossorial skink in decaying vegetation, soil and rotting wood on the forest floor (Uetz et al., 2026). Ovoviviparity is reported for this species (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The originally described female measured 71.9 mm in snout–vent length and had five digits on each limb, 24 midbody scale rows, eight lamellae beneath the fourth toe, 31 presacral vertebrae and three pairs of enlarged chin shields (Siler et al., 2012; Uetz et al., 2026). The Graceful Short-legged Skink is documented on Basilan within the Greater Mindanao PAIC. It has additional historical records from the Sulu Archipelago, outside this volume’s geographic scope (Siler et al., 2012; Uetz et al., 2026). The Sulu Slender Skink is associated with forest habitats. Its reported range includes Basilan within Greater Mindanao and other Sulu islands outside the PAIC. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.b: ◆ Philippine endemic     •     ◉ IUCN DD     •     ✦ Exceptionally rare
records.p: Reported specimens are 61.6–75.5 mm snout–vent length with five digits on each limb and 26 scale rows at midbody (Uetz et al., 2026). The Tiboli Slender Skink is recorded from southern Mindanao, including South Cotabato and Sarangani. Reports farther north in Misamis Oriental and from Dinagat require confirmation under current species limits (Pitogo et al., 2021; Sanguila et al., 2016; GBIF.org, 2026). The Tiboli Slender Skink has been found beneath decaying logs in secondary forest in South Cotabato (Uetz et al., 2026). The holotype was collected beneath a rotting log in secondary-growth forest in South Cotabato in October 2009, with further material recorded from Misamis Oriental (Siler et al., 2012). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A published skink comparison reports 59–63 middorsal scales and 17–22 lamellae below the fourth toe in Dasia semicincta, with the prefrontal scales usually separated. These specimen characters distinguish it from the Dasia grisea specimen compared in that study, but do not form a complete regional identification key (Geissler & Kupfer, 2019). The Half-banded Tree Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Sinaka (GBIF.org, 2026). The Half-banded Tree Skink is broadly associated with forests. Dasia semicincta was originally described as Euprepes (Tiliqua) semicinctus and later appeared as Dasia olivaceum semicincta. The surviving syntype identifiers include ZMB 5689 and NMW 9818; because the historical names mix species and subspecies concepts, older records require explicit name-concept matching (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The Mangrove Skink is moderately slender, with smooth overlapping scales and a greyish-brown dorsum that may bear pale spots. A subdued to darker lateral stripe runs along the flanks, and some individuals have orange ventral colouring. Colour varies across populations, so the description is a recognition guide rather than a stand-alone diagnostic key (National Parks Board Singapore, 2019). The Mangrove Skink has records from Mindanao, Dinagat, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Davao del Sur. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). This skink is recorded in coastal and mangrove vegetation, including shoreline substrates exposed to saline conditions (Uetz et al., 2026). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A University of Guam herpetofaunal guide describes juveniles and females with three pale longitudinal dorsal stripes and a blue tail, whereas adult males may become largely brown with only faint anterior stripes. This is an external-range comparative diagnosis and has not been validated for a sampled Mindanao series (Kerr, 2013). This skink lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The Pacific Blue-tailed Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga Peninsula (Smithsonian Institution, n.d.; GBIF.org, 2026). The Pacific Blue-tailed Skink is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A golden stripe runs along the dark back but does not continue onto the conspicuously reddish-orange tail (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Red-tailed Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Busa Mountain Range, Agusan del Sur, and Sarangani (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-tailed Skink is associated with forests and waterways. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The identity of this skink is based on type material from the Agusan region and its original description of body pattern and head scalation (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: Alcala’s Sun Skink has comparatively smooth head scales and a pale to white chin. Compared with its close relative E. rugifera, it also has more lamellae beneath the fourth toe and approximately equal-length third and fourth fingers. These characters are part of the original differential diagnosis (Barley et al., 2021). Alcala’s Rough-scaled Sun Skink is documented from the Pasonanca region of the Zamboanga Peninsula, western Mindanao (Barley et al., 2021). The species has been collected in low-elevation mature forest and regenerating rainforest within Pasonanca Natural Park near Zamboanga City (Barley et al., 2021). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Caraga Sun Skink is a medium-sized, bronze-to-olive skink with dark sides, a long interparietal scale separating the parietals, and five to ten moderately developed keels on each dorsal body scale. It closely resembles E. multicarinata; a greater total number of toe lamellae is helpful in comparisons, but some counts overlap (Barley et al., 2020). The Caraga Sun Skink has been reported from Mindanao, Samar and Bohol, with Mindanao localities in the northeastern mountains and Agusan del Sur. Recent specimen-based records include Agusan Marsh, while older identifications in the Eutropis complex remain less certain (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Sanguila et al., 2026). The Caraga Sun Skink is broadly associated with forests and freshwater wetlands in the working regional checklist. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Copper Sun Skink has a bronze back, dark flanks, and conspicuously keeled dorsal body scales, usually with nine to twelve keels per scale. The original key distinguishes it from related southern Philippine forms partly by a single primary temporal scale, but its diagnosis rests on limited material (Barley et al., 2020). The Copper Sun Skink is documented from South Cotabato, southern Mindanao. A population reported from the Busa Mountain Range in Sarangani has been provisionally identified as this species because of its resemblance to Eutropis caraga (Barley et al., 2020; Pitogo et al., 2021). The regional checklist groups Eutropis cuprea with shrublands. Since published observations from Mount Busa included provisional identification against E. caraga, these data should not be treated as verified evidence of habitat breadth for E. cuprea. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Mindanao Six-striped Sun Skink has five dark longitudinal stripes across the back, alternating with pale lines, and broad brown bands along the sides. A bluish throat has been described in living individuals. This contrasting pattern helps distinguish it from other Philippine sun skinks (Barley et al., 2020; Pitogo et al., 2020; Tirona et al., 2023). The Mindanao Six-striped Sun Skink is documented from Sarangani and North Cotabato in Mindanao. Historical reports from Mount Hamiguitan and specimens formerly assigned to this species near Digos have been questioned, so these remain disputed localities (Pitogo et al., 2020; Barley et al., 2020; Tirona et al., 2023; GBIF.org, 2026). Field observations from Sarangani and North Cotabato place this skink along lowland forest edges, agricultural margins and disturbed residential vegetation. Individuals have been observed in grass and leaf litter, sheltering in crevices and basking on rocks or concrete (Pitogo et al., 2020; Tirona et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Striking Philippine Sun Skink has a bronze-to-olive back and a sharply bounded dark band along each side, contrasting with a pale underside. The crisp lower edge of the lateral band helps distinguish it from E. caraga and E. multicarinata, which have a more mottled transition toward the belly (Barley et al., 2020). This skink is documented from the forests of Eastern Samar, including the Balangiga region (Barley et al., 2020). The Striking Philippine Sun Skink is listed from streams and rivers in the working checklist, without distinguishing waterside vegetation from aquatic habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Lapulapu’s Sun Skink is a relatively small, slender skink with a broad dark band along each side and five to nine keels on its dorsal body scales. Adult males may show orange coloration around the head or front of the body. Its small size and generally lower toe-lamella counts help separate it from the similar, often co-occurring E. caraga (Barley et al., 2020). Lapulapu’s Sun Skink has records from Mindanao and Samar, including Agusan del Sur and Eastern Samar. Recent specimen-based records place it in the Agusan Marsh area (Barley et al., 2020; Sanguila et al., 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Lapulapu's Sun Skink is associated with forests and freshwater wetlands. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Many-keeled Sun Skink is a medium-sized bronze-to-brown skink with darker flanks and usually indistinct pale striping. Its interparietal scale separates the parietals. It is morphologically similar to E. caraga, but typically has fewer toe lamellae, with counts overlapping near the boundary (Barley et al., 2020). The Many-keeled Sun Skink has been reported from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte and Dinagat. Some historical records predate revisions to the Eutropis multicarinata species complex and may reflect broader earlier identifications (Beukema, 2011; Sanguila et al., 2016; Barley et al., 2020; GBIF.org, 2026). The Many-keeled Sun Skink has been recorded in ground-level and aquatic habitats on northeastern Leyte (Decena et al., 2023). This skink lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Leyte observers recorded daytime basking on partly open ground and leaf litter and noted individuals entering the water when disturbed (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The Many-lined Sun Skink is a relatively large, robust skink with an olive-brown to gray back, dark dorsolateral markings, and mostly weakly three-keeled dorsal scales. Its larger size and weaker, fewer keels help separate it from several smaller Philippine Eutropis species (Barley et al., 2020; Sanguila et al., 2026). The Many-lined Sun Skink is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park, Mount Huraw, and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). Recorded across forest edges, settlements and other disturbed landscapes (Sanguila et al., 2016). A Taguibo Watershed survey near Butuan City, eastern Mindanao, recorded these skinks on the ground within its terrestrial sampling zone (Sanguila et al., 2021). Ovoviviparous reproduction is recorded in the taxonomic literature (Uetz et al., 2026). In northeastern Leyte, observers recorded three skinks in degraded pasture. Individuals moved across sandy riparian ground around midday and through grasses at night (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A predominantly green, tree-climbing skink; the scientific epithet smaragdina refers to an emerald-green appearance (Uetz et al., 2026). The Emerald Tree Skink has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; GIZ, 2013). Specimens were observed on coconut palms in coastal plantations (Sanguila et al., 2016).

The herrei form shows paired, unfused frontoparietal scales (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Taylor's Lipinia is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Taylor's Lipinia is associated with forests. The Reptile Database recognizes auriculata, herrei and kempi within Lipinia auriculata. Mindanao records described by Sanguila and colleagues (2016) use the herrei name (Sanguila et al., 2016; Uetz et al., 2026).

This small, slender skink has a yellow stripe along the pale-brown back, long digits, and a visible external ear opening (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Beautiful Lipinia has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; GIZ, 2013). Reported on branches and mats of epiphytic vegetation (Sanguila et al., 2016).

A slender tree skink with four dark longitudinal lines running along its brown back (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Four-striped Slender Tree Skink has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Pasonanca area, Taguibo Watershed, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Individuals were found on tree bark and ferns above inundated peat-swamp ground (Sanguila et al., 2026). Recorded among trunk mosses, epiphytic mats and arboreal ferns (Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in vegetation and trees (Sanguila et al., 2021). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A relatively robust skink with four dark longitudinal stripes that fade toward the rear of the body. The tympanum is exposed (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Semper's Slender Tree Skink has records from Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). A single 1982 specimen was collected during daylight from an epiphytic fern about 4 m above the ground in primary forest at roughly 800 m elevation in eastern Mindanao. One arboreal encounter demonstrates observed microhabitat use, not exclusive reliance on epiphytes (Smith, 1993). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

r.full: Smith, B. E. (1993). Notes on a collection of squamate reptiles from eastern Mindanao, Philippine Islands. Part 1: Lacertilia. Asiatic Herpetological Research, 5, 85–95.

records.p: A published comparative review describes this striped skink as having longitudinal dorsal stripes that extend forward to the forelimb region, 22 scale rows around midbody, and a reported snout–vent length of 47–56 mm. The combination is useful for comparing preserved specimens with other Lipinia species (Poyarkov et al., 2019). The Striped Slender Tree Skink has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Striped Slender Tree Skink is broadly associated with forests. The Striped Lipinia was originally described as Cophoscincus subvittatus and later transferred to Lipinia. Its type material came from Sulawesi, and the species is also listed from Mindanao (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: In a comparative taxonomic account, Lipinia vulcania has a brownish dorsum scattered with darker spots and a dark lateral stripe interrupted by whitish or yellowish spots. It is also described as having 17 lamellae beneath the fourth toe, with the forelimbs and hindlimbs failing to meet when pressed against the body (Poyarkov et al., 2019). The Girard's Slender Tree Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga Peninsula (Brown et al., 2013; Uetz et al., 2026). The Girard's Slender Tree Skink is broadly associated with forests. Historical museum literature discusses an early USNM specimen proposed as a possible type of Lipinia vulcania, following an earlier identification under another Girard name (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A small, smooth-scaled skink recorded in a comparative species synopsis at up to 44.5 mm snout–vent length, with a distinct external ear opening, 24 scale rows around midbody, 54 longitudinal scales from the parietals to the tail base and 20 lamellae beneath the fourth toe. The dorsal surface was characterized as greenish with a brown iridescent sheen. These are the reported morphological characters for Lipinia zamboangensis in Das and Austin (2007), which cites earlier Philippine treatments. Other Lipinia share parts of this combination, so a firm identification should compare multiple scalation characters; the original 1963 description was not independently reexamined here. The Zamboanga Slender Tree Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Malindang Range, Zamboanga Peninsula, and Misamis Occidental (Uetz et al., 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Zamboanga Slender Tree Skink is associated with forests. The Reptile Database lists the holotype as CAS-SUR 22425, from Dapitan Peak on the Zamboanga Peninsula, and records the original combination Lygosoma (Leiolopisma) zamboangensis Brown & Alcala, 1963. The type locality establishes specimen provenance, not a present-day abundance or a range-wide elevation interval (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Tinuy-an account describes large, robust adults with distinctive head scalation (Plaza et al., 2025). A large-bodied skink distinguished by its robust, elongated build (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Cuming's Eared Skink is recorded on Leyte and Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013; GBIF.org, 2026). The Cuming's Eared Skink is associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The published diagnosis records snout–vent lengths around 50–60 mm, fused frontoparietal scales and 34–38 scale rows at midbody (Uetz et al., 2026). The small anterior loreal scale is triangular and does not meet the upper lip scales (Uetz et al., 2026). The Mt. Kitanglad Forest Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Hilong-Hilong, and Surigao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026). Recorded from forested, high-altitude mountain plateau habitat (Sanguila et al., 2016). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This very small skink has a short, blunt snout, large eyes, and a dark-brown body, often with pale dorsolateral stripes or blotches (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Steere's Forest Skink has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Zamboanga del Norte, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Collected in woody litter beneath tree buttresses around 700–900 m (Sanguila et al., 2016). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The diagnosis notes paired frontoparietal head scales and 19–26 lamellae beneath the fourth toe; the prominent dark bars below the eyes of P. jagori are absent (Uetz et al., 2026). The Philippine Giant Forest Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Lumot, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). Observed along riparian margins and agricultural–forest boundaries (Sanguila et al., 2016). Older Philippine treatments used the name Sphenomorphus abdictus and discussed overlapping Sphenomorphus jagori usages (Uetz et al., 2026).

Taylor’s published diagnosis, reproduced by The Reptile Database, describes a single frontoparietal scale, separated prefrontals, five supraoculars and yellow spots on the three posterior upper labials. When the hindlimb is pressed forward it does not reach beyond the forelimb elbow. This combination contrasts with the paired frontoparietals described for P. mindanensis (The Reptile Database, 2026). The Cox's Sphenomorphus has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Magdiwata, and Misamis Occidental. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The 2016 inventory records animals at low- and middle-elevation forest edges (Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in ground-level habitats (Sanguila et al., 2021). Oviparity is listed for this species (Uetz et al., 2026).

The Agusan Marsh treatment describes a medium-sized terrestrial skink with robust hindlimbs and variable dark markings on a brown back. These variable markings should not be treated as a conclusive field diagnosis because distinct genetic lineages have been reported among populations assigned to this species (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Jagor's Sphenomorphus has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Reported from lowland forests and disturbed habitats around 500–600 m (Sanguila et al., 2016). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026).

The northeastern Leyte account describes a large riparian skink, approximately 70–90 mm snout–vent length, with dark-brown to blackish dorsal coloration and mottled scales (Decena et al., 2023). The Eastern Visayas Forest Skink is recorded on Samar and Leyte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Eastern Visayas Forest Skink has been recorded in ground-level and aquatic habitats on northeastern Leyte (Decena et al., 2023). At the Leyte sites, individuals were active along streams by day and escaped disturbance by swimming or sheltering in streamside boulder crevices (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The original diagnosis of the Mindanao Sphenomorphus notes paired frontoparietal scales with an intervening interparietal, a scaly lower eyelid, about 32 scales around the midbody and a small ear opening. The fore- and hindlimbs barely touch when pressed against the body. These are specimen-level characters rather than quick field marks (The Reptile Database, 2026, after Taylor 1915). The Mindanao Forest Skink has been reported from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte and Bohol. Mindanao records include its northern and northeastern mountains, while the southern Busa Mountain Range population was provisionally identified as Pinoyscincus cf. mindanensis (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2021). Survey records placed this skink in upper-elevation mountain forest (Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in ground-level habitats (Sanguila et al., 2021). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A forest skink that can be assessed through scale counts rather than coloration alone. In Linkem, Diesmos and Brown’s (2010) comparative table, the examined S. acutus material has a reported snout–vent length range of 51–76 mm, 26–30 scales around midbody, 51–61 paravertebral scales and 28–36 lamellae under the fourth toe. These data contrast with S. variegatus, which the same comparative study reports as having 38–44 midbody scales, 66–76 paravertebral scales and 19–25 fourth-toe lamellae. The numerical combinations are particularly useful for separating those two species in hand, but the original comparative series are limited and possible overlap with additional Philippine forest skinks needs direct key-based assessment. Do not identify an animal on apparent pointed snout shape alone. The Pointed-snouted Forest Skink has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026). The Pointed-snouted Forest Skink was recorded in vegetation and trees in the Taguibo Watershed of Mindanao (Sanguila et al., 2021). Sleeping individuals were encountered inside rolled banana or abaca leaves (Sanguila et al., 2016). During an eastern Mindanao survey in 1982, three animals were caught by day in ground-level drift fences despite the species’ traditionally reported arboreal habits. Examined stomachs contained arachnids and orthopterans. Ground captures and prey remains are direct observations, not quantified habitat selection or diet proportions (Smith, 1993). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A high number of paravertebral scales helps distinguish this montane skink (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Fairy Forest Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017). The Fairy Forest Skink is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The elongated body has smooth, unkeeled dorsal scales, narrow pale crossbands across a dark back, and a tail that is thickened near its base (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Banded Forest Skink has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; Beukema, 2011). The Banded Forest Skink uses coastal lowland forest, regrowth and disturbed land. One eastern Mindanao specimen contained several kinds of insect prey (Sanguila et al., 2016; Smith, 1993). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A forest skink distinguishable from similar nominal Sphenomorphus by a combination of scale characters. The Philippine comparative table of Linkem, Diesmos and Brown (2010) reports a 49–63 mm snout–vent length range, 38–44 midbody scale rows, 66–76 paravertebral scales, and 19–25 fourth-toe lamellae for S. variegatus. In the same study S. acutus instead has 26–30 midbody rows, 51–61 paravertebrals and 28–36 fourth-toe lamellae. The differences are useful for identifying preserved or carefully examined animals, rather than being assured in a distant sighting. Sample counts and taxonomic treatments may differ among sources, so multiple characters and locality-supported voucher comparisons remain necessary before assigning difficult records. The Variegated Forest Skink has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026). Northeast Mindanao records came from low-elevation original and regenerating forests (Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in ground-level habitats (Sanguila et al., 2021). In the 1982 eastern Mindanao collection, females taken on 11 April and 24 May each had two oviductal eggs; juveniles measured 24–39 mm snout–vent length. Most records were in primary forest, with two in late secondary forest. These figures describe the sampled animals and dates only (Smith, 1993). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A slender, relatively long-bodied skink with short limbs and smooth, glossy brownish dorsal scales; lateral surfaces may be finely speckled. A regional identification guide describes a transparent lower-eyelid disc, midbody scale rows numbering 24–28 and 13–14 lamellae below the fourth toe, with measured adult snout–vent lengths around 50–57 mm in its Myanmar specimen series. The coloration and dimensions reported from mainland Southeast Asia should not be assumed to diagnose every Philippine animal: the published guide itself warns of evidence for a wider bowringii species complex. Where inherited Greater Mindanao records are concerned, locality, introduction history and voucher confirmation remain separate unresolved questions (Tanintharyi field guide; Ecology Asia). Bowring’s Supple Skink has a historical report from Zamboanga, western Mindanao, interpreted as a probable introduction. Reports from the Sulu Archipelago belong to a different faunal region (Ross, 1989; Uetz et al., 2026). The Bowring's Agile Skink is broadly associated with forests. Older literature placed this skink in Lygosoma and Riopa before its assignment to Subdoluseps (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

r.full: Ross, C. A. (1989). Probable introduction of Lygosoma bowringi in Zamboanga City, Philippines. Herpetological Review, 20(1), 6.

records.p: Diagnostic features include usually separate prefrontal scales, a single preanal shield, 34–41 midbody scale rows and two superposed anterior loreal scales (Uetz et al., 2026). The Davao Keeled Water Skink is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Busa Mountain Range, Davao Oriental, and Sarangani (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; Uetz et al., 2026). The original collection locality was beside a quiet stream near sea level in the Caburan area of southern Mindanao (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Leyte field account describes prominent, dark, spiny scales along the dorsum, rather than the smoother body surface of some other sympatric skinks (Decena et al., 2023). The Philippine Keeled Water Skink has records from Samar and Leyte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). A semi-aquatic forest skink commonly associated with running water and streamside rocks (Uetz et al., 2026). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in terrestrial microhabitats (Decena et al., 2023). In northeastern Leyte, three skinks sheltered beneath dead wood or streamside rocks. At handling, one response noted was immobility resembling death-feigning (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The skink has low-keel dorsal scales, smooth head shields and 28–34 scale rows around the body (Plaza et al., 2025). The Misamis Keeled Water Skink is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Cabadbaran–Santiago forest, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Lumot, and Surigao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026; Uetz et al., 2026). Observed submerged in shallow water or sheltered among stream rocks and litter (Plaza et al., 2025). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in ground-level habitats (Sanguila et al., 2021). Streamside skinks retreated beneath flowing water when approached (Sanguila et al., 2016). At a lower Mt. Kitanglad stream, two individuals were seen swimming at night and a juvenile was found in daytime among large streambed rocks (Beukema, 2011). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The Mt. Kitanglad identification comparison records dusky-brown coloration, seven pale dorsal cross-bands, and raised, backward-pointing spines on the tail scales (Beukema, 2011). The Partello's Keeled Water Skink has records from Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Magdiwata, Misamis Occidental, and Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011). Recorded on forested streambanks among wet rocks and logs (Sanguila et al., 2016). A single individual was observed hiding in a crevice in a steep, partially vegetated stream bank in the lower Mt. Kitanglad Range (Beukema, 2011). A single Mt. Kitanglad skink was found in daylight concealed in a crevice in a steep, partly vegetated stream bank (Beukema, 2011). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The head has four large supraocular shields, separate frontoparietal scales, and no supranasal shields; the fourth toe is only slightly longer than the third (Uetz et al., 2026). The Zamboanga Forest Skink has been documented on Mindanao and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area and Zamboanga del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Zamboanga Forest Skink is associated with forests. This skink was originally named Sphenomorphus atrigularis in 1908 and subsequently assigned to Tytthoscincus. The original holotype was collected at the base of the Malindang Mountains in 1906, providing an anchored historic Mindanao record rather than recent survey evidence (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).
