records.p: Tytthoscincus biparietalis is assigned to a group of very small skinks, usually below 45 mm snout–vent length, with small temporal scales that blend with the surrounding body scales and a fourth toe only about as long as, or slightly longer than, the third. This species shares divided parietal head scales with T. hallieri, a feature cited in transferring it from Sphenomorphus to Tytthoscincus. The cited genus revision did not include molecular data for T. biparietalis; these characters support its generic placement but do not, by themselves, uniquely diagnose the species (Linkem et al., 2011). The Sulu Forest Skink has records from Basilan (Uetz et al., 2026; Museum of Comparative Zoology, n.d.). The Sulu Forest Skink is associated with forests. Originally described as Sphenomorphus biparietalis in 1918, this species was subsequently transferred to Tytthoscincus. Its original holotype from Lapac Island in the Sulu Archipelago was reportedly destroyed during World War II; later identifications should recognize this type-material limitation (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: This small blindsnake has a pale snout, chin and tail tip; the distinctive nasal scale sutures help separate it from other blindsnakes (Uetz et al., 2026). The Brahminy Worm Snake is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Agad-Agad, Zamboanga del Norte, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022). Recorded beneath logs and stones around buildings and gardens (Sanguila et al., 2016). A triploid parthenogenetic egg-laying snake; females can produce offspring without males (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Philippine identification key describes Malayotyphlops ruber as lacking a pale collar behind the head and having fewer than 400 transverse scale rows between head and tail. Its dark dorsal stripe covers 15 scale rows across the anterior body, compared with 13 rows in the similar M. andyi (Weinell et al., 2019). The Red Worm Snake is documented on Samar (Uetz et al., 2026). The Red Worm Snake is broadly associated with forests. Leviton and colleagues’ Philippine snake catalogue gives Samar Island as the historical type locality of Malayotyphlops ruber (originally Typhlops ruber), with holotype SMF 16616. Its treatment retains Samar distribution and identifies unresolved comparisons among Malayotyphlops populations; the type record is historical evidence, not a contemporary occupancy survey (Leviton et al., 2018). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Philippine snake key separates Ramphotyphlops cumingii from its congeners by a third supralabial scale overlapping the ocular scale and by 24–28 longitudinal body-scale rows at midbody. The first character separates it from R. marxi, whereas the higher scale-row count separates it from the other species treated in the key (Weinell et al., 2019). The Cuming's Worm Snake has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Agusan del Norte, and Davao Oriental. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017). The Cuming's Worm Snake is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: Two newly reported Samar voucher specimens measured 160 and 264 mm snout–vent length. Both had a broad, parallel-sided, beaked rostral, 30 midbody scale rows and pointed tails representing approximately 5% and 7.5% of total length. These are measurements of two specimens, not a species-wide size range (Diesmos et al., 2026). The Marx's Worm Snake has been documented on Samar, including Samar Island Natural Park (Diesmos et al., 2026). A recent Samar Island Natural Park survey reported additional living specimens of the blind snake in limestone-associated forest, including animals encountered above ground on saplings. These observations document where the specimens were found, but are insufficient to establish arboreal habitat selection or typical activity patterns (Diesmos et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Comparative diagnostic treatments have reported approximately 20 midbody scale rows for Ramphotyphlops olivaceus, versus 18 in Gerrhopilus hedraeus and 22 in R. suluensis. Such minute snakes often require careful scale counts and expert review because gross brown coloration is insufficient (Uetz et al., 2026). The Olive Worm Snake is documented on Basilan and Samar within Greater Mindanao. Mainland Mindanao has been suggested from aggregated records but is not confirmed in the specialist treatment; additional reports from the Sulu Archipelago are outside the PAIC (Leviton et al., 2018; GBIF.org, 2026). The Olive Worm Snake is associated with forests. The broad classification does not establish soil, litter, or other retreat sites at named Greater Mindanao localities. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).
